This tutorial connects ordinary mathematical writing to a small explicit
catalogue. Render the article, follow a glossary link, then change one label.
The later sections explain its assumption and two authored proof relations.

## 1. Render the article

In this source folder, open `example.qmd` and use your editor's **Render** or
**Preview** command. From a terminal you can instead run:

```sh
quarto render example.qmd --to html
```

If working in another folder, first follow `README.md` to install the extension,
then copy **both** `example.qmd` and `knowledge.json` there. A GitHub installation
uses `filters: [kai-prince-sfhea/maths-knowledge-graph]`; this source example uses
the local `filters: [maths-knowledge-graph]` route.

The result should show a numbered definition and theorem, followed by a
**Mathematical glossary** with links back to their source text. No AI model or
companion extension is required for this first render.

## 2. Read the native mathematical source

The next blocks use ordinary Quarto theorem syntax. The catalogue supplies
explicit identities and relations; it does not change their mathematical text.

::: {#def-square name="Square of a real number" am-macro="amSquare" am-args="value" am-intent="square($value)" am-tex="(#1)^2"}
The [square]{#concept-square} of a real number $x$ is the product $x\cdot x$,
written $x^2$.
:::

::: {#thm-square name="Positive squares"}
For every nonzero real number $x$, the square $x^2$ is positive.
:::

The term is defined in @def-square. [Read the assumptions](#assumption-real),
[follow the proof by signs](#prf-sign), or
[follow the proof using absolute value](#prf-absolute) for @thm-square.

## 3. Follow the mathematical glossary

::: {#maths-glossary .maths-glossary}
:::

Select **Positive squares** in this glossary to return to the theorem. Follow
**Square** to its defining term. The entries come from the catalogue's explicit
public objects and real source anchors, not matching words elsewhere on the page.

## 4. Change one label and render again

Open `knowledge.json` and find the object whose `id` is
`math:positive-square`. Change its English label from `Positive squares` to
`Square positivity`, then render `example.qmd` again. The glossary label should
change, while the theorem retains its authored **Positive squares** name and
the same mathematical statement. Leave its ID and source anchor unchanged.

If a catalogue-only edit does not refresh in Preview, run Render again. The
README also explains the local candidate's literal YAML catalogue support;
there is no author-written conversion script.

## 5. Inspect the authored assumption and proofs

The catalogue links the theorem to the following assumption with `assumes` and
links each proof to its statement with `proves`. Each proof's status is
`unverified`: these are authored associations, not formal checking results.
You can inspect their IDs, source anchors and relations in `knowledge.json`.

### Assumption

::: {#assumption-real .am-assumption am-summary="Assumption: a nonzero real input"}
The input $x$ belongs to the ordered field of real numbers and satisfies $x\ne0$.
The nonzero condition excludes the case $x^2=0$.
:::

### Proof by signs

::: {#prf-sign .proof am-summary="Proof by signs"}
If $x>0$, the product $x\cdot x$ is positive. If $x<0$, then $-x>0$,
so $x^2=(-x)\cdot(-x)>0$. A nonzero real number has one of these two signs.
:::

### Proof using absolute value

::: {#prf-absolute .proof am-summary="Proof using absolute value"}
For a nonzero real number $x$, its absolute value satisfies $|x|>0$.
The product of two positive real numbers is positive, so $|x|^2>0$.
Since $|x|^2=x^2$, the conclusion follows.
:::

## 6. Try the paired QMD-only authoring route

If you have also installed the local Accessible Maths 0.0.9 candidate, create
a new `native-glossary.qmd` in your own project. Copy the small article below,
then use ordinary **Render**. This route needs no separate knowledge file:

```markdown
---
title: My native mathematical glossary
filters: [maths-knowledge-graph, accessible-maths]
accessible-maths:
  catalogue: true
maths-knowledge-graph:
  scopes: [algebra]
---

::: {#def-native-square name="Square" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/native-square" am-review="author-reviewed" am-public="true" am-scope="algebra"}
For a real number $x$, its square is $x\cdot x$.
:::

::: {.maths-glossary}
:::
```

Follow **Square** back to the definition. Edit its `name` in that QMD and render
again: the glossary updates on that same render. The attributes explicitly
declare identity, review, publication and knowledge context; they do not prove
the mathematical statement. Keep the filter order shown. Use owner-qualified
filter names for GitHub installations; the currently published versions are
earlier than this local candidate pair.

To add navigation, install the compatible local Knowledge Graph Extraction
candidate in that project and select its filter after the two shown above:

```yaml
filters: [maths-knowledge-graph, accessible-maths, knowledge-graph-extraction]
```

Render the whole project. A separate **Mathematics** graph appears after the
mathematical content, and KG's website search includes its public records. Drag
a node or use the graph's text and keyboard controls. The README explains graph
names, placement and search options. Your original `example.qmd` remains a
standalone catalogue tutorial and needs no companion for its normal render.

## 7. Choose your next step

Select Accessible Maths **after** Maths Knowledge Graph if you want these
declared proof and assumption associations to become authored disclosures.
Knowledge Graph Extraction adds a separate project-wide graph and navigation;
it is optional for this page-local tutorial. See `README.md` for the complete
filter order and shared-catalogue configuration.

For approved reader notation choices and cross-page preferences, try the
[`examples/notation` website](examples/notation/index.qmd). The README explains
[page defaults, required notation and portable preferences](README.md#page-defaults-required-notation-and-portable-preferences),
the [optional controlled-English proof candidate](README.md#optional-controlled-english-proof-candidates)
experiment, [ordinary-prose proposals and constructive subproofs](README.md#ordinary-prose-private-proposals-and-reviewed-public-output),
and [qualified relation reuse](README.md#qualified-relation-reuse).
These are separate next steps; the tutorial above needs none of them.

You can also render the full authored content to Word:

```sh
quarto render example.qmd --to docx
```

[The catalogue is explicit; matching words do not create new identities.]{#catalogue-note}

The glossary records authored associations and proof statuses. Its prerequisite
links describe reading dependencies; a path through them is not a mathematical
proof. This example and its original synthetic catalogue use Apache License 2.0.
